member.name: P:__CSharpShellAspNetHost.ApplicationName
member.summary: The application name ASP.NET Core would normally take from the entry assembly.
member.remarks: It has to be stated because there is no entry assembly to take it from: this program was loaded from a stream into a collectible load context, so Assembly.GetEntryAssembly() returns null and the name defaults to "". Two things then break — hosting startup scanning throws ArgumentException("The value cannot be an empty string"), and MVC's application-part discovery finds no parts, which silently 404s every Razor Page and every component in the app. This type is compiled into the user's own assembly, so its name is exactly the name a `dotnet run` would have used.

member.name: M:__CSharpShellHttpListenerServer.#ctor(Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration.IConfiguration)
member.summary: Takes the app's configuration so the endpoint a Kestrel project already declares is the endpoint this server binds - see ResolveConfiguredAddresses.

member.name: M:__CSharpShellHttpListenerServer.ResolveConfiguredAddresses
member.summary: The addresses this app's configuration asks for, when ASP.NET Core's own "urls" key said nothing. Empty when the configuration says nothing either.
member.remarks:
Three shapes are read, most standard first:
Kestrel:Endpoints:{name}:Url - what a real Kestrel project already declares, so swapping this server in for Kestrel keeps a project's appsettings.json working. Every endpoint is taken, in the order they are written.
Kestrel:EndpointDefaults:Url - Kestrel's own fallback for endpoints that name no URL of their own.
Server:Url(s) and WebServer:Url(s) - a plainer place to say it for a project that was never a Kestrel project.
Anything holding several addresses may separate them with ';', as the "urls" key does.

member.name: M:__CSharpShellHttpListenerServer.Bind(System.Collections.Generic.List{System.String})
member.summary: Starts the listener, falling back to a free ephemeral port when the requested one is taken. Without the fallback, running twice after a crash — where the previous listener has not released :5000 yet — fails with a bare HttpListenerException and nothing the user could act on.

member.name: M:__CSharpShellHttpListenerServer.Normalize(System.String)
member.summary: HttpListener wants a prefix, not a URL: the trailing slash is mandatory, and the several spellings of "every interface" have to become the one HttpListener recognises.
member.remarks: Any other host the user asked for is kept. Every host used to be rewritten to 127.0.0.1, which quietly made "http://0.0.0.0:8080" - the whole point of which is to be reachable from another machine - loopback-only. Binding every interface can still fail, and Bind falls back to a free loopback port when it does.

member.name: M:__CSharpShellHttpListenerServer.Reported(System.String)
member.summary: The same prefix as an address to report. A wildcard host is reported as 0.0.0.0 — which is what Kestrel reports for the same binding, and what a `dotnet run` prints.
member.remarks: It used to be reported as localhost, which was openable but hid the one fact that matters: whether the app is loopback-only or reachable from the network. Nothing but the app itself knows that, so it has to be said here — the IDE reads 0.0.0.0 as "every interface" and expands it to this device's real addresses for its banner (ListeningAddress.Expand). A non-wildcard prefix is already the answer and is kept.

member.name: M:__CSharpShellHttpListenerServer.Track(System.Threading.Tasks.Task)
member.summary: Remembers a request while it runs, so StopAsync can drain what is still in flight.
member.remarks: A discarded task is not a free-standing thing: while it runs, its state machine is on the thread pool and every frame in it belongs to this program's load context. Leaving one behind therefore keeps the whole context alive after the run ends — and a Blazor circuit always leaves one, because SignalR's long-polling transport parks a GET on the server for as long as it is allowed to. The IDE then has two copies of this program loaded on the next run, which is exactly the state where a component "does not implement IComponent".

member.name: M:__CSharpShellResponseFeature.StartAsync(System.Threading.CancellationToken)
member.summary: Sends the status line and headers, once. Everything registered through OnStarting runs first and in reverse registration order, which is the order ASP.NET Core middleware expects: the callback added last is the innermost one and must see the response first.

member.name: T:__CSharpShellResponseStream
member.summary: The response body, wrapped so the headers are sent on the first byte written rather than eagerly. Middleware routinely sets a header after calling the next one in the pipeline, and sending the status line before the pipeline has finished would silently drop those.
